section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Narrative Writing Overview and Standards
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary

In most states, the argumentative and informative writing standards are placed BEFORE narrative writing, reflecting their higher priority. And while we typically target narrative writing LESS than the other two, we have to recognize the relevance of storytelling skills used in various careers. For example, police officers document incidents, healthcare professionals gather patient histories, and video game designers create engaging storylines. The ability to think and communicate narratively IS a vital skill in many professions. Given this, while the narrative writing standard may be third in line, it should not be overlooked instructionally.

Narrative writing includes many different genres — some we tend to read and some we tend to write. For example: A Personal Narrative is a true story about one's own experience. Realistic Fiction is a made-up story that COULD happen in real life. Fantasy involves magical or supernatural elements. A Play or Drama is a story written in script form and told through performance. And a Memoir highlights a SELECT experience from one's own life, written with a heavy dose of reflection and personal insight.

More unique narrative genres include stories written in RESPONSE to a text read. For example: After reading literature, continue the story by imagining what happens next or exploring a future event. After reading a story, you can retell it from another character's perspective. You could also write Fiction Based on Fact, creating a fictional story inspired by information learned from nonfiction texts.

Now your state standards likely don't name the specific types or genres you are to tackle. Rather they more broadly state that you are to TEACH students HOW to compose or write narratives.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Grade-Level Standards and Four Essential Skills
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Standards and Essential Skills

Let's look at a couple grade-level standards for instructional expectations:

6th GRADE, in most states, reads something like this: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events. Orient the reader by establishing a context and introducing a narrator and/or characters. Organize an event sequence using dialogue, pacing, and description, to develop events and characters. Provide a conclusion that follows and reflects on the narrated experiences or events.

As we jump up and look at the 8th grade writing standard, it's essentially the same with an added expectation of character REFLECTION. All grade levels are building on one another. And by high school, there is the addition of developing MULTIPLE PLOT LINES and building toward a TONE.

For most teachers, the skills outlined in the standards are likely familiar — but there are a lot of them! And since narrative writing is intentionally listed as the third mode of writing and is often taught-and-practiced less frequently, let's prioritize the 4 most essential skills to teach:

1. Develop a conflict
2. Reflect and resolve the situation
3. Introduce character and setting/context
4. Use narrative techniques to sequence the details

Throughout this episode, we will look closely at these 4 essential ingredients of narrative writing and the key points to make within your Tier 1 whole-class mini-lessons.
skill_title: Grade-Level Standards and Four Essential Skills

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Skill 1: Develop a Conflict
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Skill #1: Develop a Conflict

It is a common MISCONCEPTION that narrative writing is the easiest of the three writing modes. In reality, conveying information and arguing an idea tend to come more naturally to students. Narrative writing requires more than just TELLING the reader something — the writer has to take the reader on a ride through the story arc. And this does NOT come naturally to students.

Using an airplane analogy: the story begins on the runway establishing the main character and setting, then it takes off when the conflict is revealed. However, one of the biggest weaknesses in students' narrative writing is often its lack of conflict. Rather, they provide lots of details about characters: Who they are, what they look like, where they go, what they do, who they talk to. But there is no conflict. The story never takes off.

The character is not the main idea of a narrative. The problem he faces is. For a story to work, something has to happen to someone. This is what is meant by an "event or experience" in the standards. The conflict or problem is the foundation of a narrative and therefore should be the first skill we teach as part of narrative writing instruction.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Three Types of Conflict
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Three Types of Conflict

Now we can't just TELL students to include a problem in their narratives, we need to TEACH them how. And while there are limitless problems a character could face, they all fall under one of three broad categories. The main character can have a conflict with: someONE, someTHING, or himSELF. We can help students remember their 3 options by pairing each one with an emoji.

The main character can have a problem with someONE, referring to an individual or group. In literature, we identify this conflict as character VS character or character VS society. Within these stories, the writer describes WHO caused the main character to be so upset and WHY.

Or the main character can have a problem with someTHING. This may include a physical obstacle like the weather or failed technology, or an unavoidable situation. In literature, we refer to these conflicts as character v nature, character v the environment, or character v technology.

Or the main character's problem can stem from himself — Character VS self. These conflicts describe a character's internal struggle with his own thoughts, beliefs, morals, or desires.

When teaching these types of conflict to your WRITERS, return to literature you have READ. As you introduce the categories of conflict that they COULD plan into their own stories, use mentor text to show them examples. Return to previously-read short stories, animated video shorts, or even popular movies. Quickly review the plot, then label each with one of the three categories. This will further solidify what you mean by stories have conflicts.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Modeling Conflict Development with Photographs
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Modeling Conflict Development with Photographs

Now it's time to model how writers come up with a story's problem. You might do this using photographs. Point out the character and setting details that are evident in the photo. For example, four people are starting on a hike. Remind students that every story has something happen that is bad, wrong, or dangerous, and yet the characters in this picture are not hurt, not upset, nothing is wrong — YET. Model how to think about what could happen, what could go wrong.

Consider possible conflicts that are realistic for THESE characters in THAT setting. For example, the four individuals are hiking and: Characters argue over food or resource sharing, OR the rocky and steep terrain is more difficult than the group expected, OR maybe one character is afraid of heights.

When first teaching students how to plan a story's problem, model the process SEVERAL times using DIFFERENT photos. Students aren't going to actually WRITE any of these stories. We are only using the photos to teach and practice HOW to come up with possible story conflicts.

After modeling several different problem possibilities, then teach students how to narrow down to ONE. Remember, this is the main idea — so the story needs to be centered around a single problem. Emphasize the importance of choosing and writing about ONE MAIN problem that the character will struggle with throughout the whole narrative.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Subplots and Personal Narrative Topics
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Subplots and Personal Narrative Topics

It may be the conflict the writer knows the most about, or is the most realistic for the situation, or is the most interesting. However, these other possible problems are potential SUBPLOTS. NOW, don't teach that concept right now. Keep students focused on the process for developing ONE main conflict. But, return to these photos and their multiple conflicts in the future, when you're ready to introduce how MULTIPLE plot lines are all intertwined.

After plenty of instruction and practice with photographs, shift the focus to identifying personal narrative topics. Encourage students to reflect on pivotal moments in their own lives — situations where they experienced strong emotions such as anger, sadness, or hurt.

Guide them to list MULTIPLE times where they struggled with someONE, with someTHING, and even with themSELVES. Have them state the CONFLICT in just a couple sentences. And knowing it's part of the story's middle, have them place it lower on the document. Provide students lots of practice with this skill by having them note the gist of each conflict for all of the TOPICS they came up with.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Skill 2: Reflect and Resolve the Situation
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Skill #2: Reflect and Resolve the Situation

After explicit instruction and plenty of guided practice in planning story problems, then transition to teaching students how to integrate a SOLUTION — and that's Essential Skill #2.

Writers must plan the ending, and that means planning how the problem gets solved. The character's problem can't keep going on and on, just like an airplane can't keep going up and up. The writer has to eventually land this problem by providing a solution or resolution. However, simply ending with "The end" or "I woke up and it was a dream" does not actually fix the problem. Such endings leave the reader dissatisfied. They come too fast, and they're not realistic. Remind students that they're writing for an audience who wants to know how the situation turned out. They need the end to include a solution.

But smooth satisfying conclusions don't just happen. Writers don't just take off with a conflict and wonder where it's going. They begin planning the end right after determining the conflict. They KNOW where their own story is going.

Again, this will require explicit instruction on the 3 TYPES of solutions:
— someONE offers help or advice
— someTHING provides a solution or fix
— OR, TIME resolves or diminishes the issue

Each of these brings the reader a sense of closure, although the ending doesn't have to FIX the problem or make it ALL better. That's the difference between a SOLUTION and a RESOLUTION.
skill_title: Skill 2: Reflect and Resolve the Situation

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Solution vs Resolution and Character Reflection
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Solution vs Resolution and Character Reflection

If the conflict is conquered, then it's a SOLUTION — a clear fix or "victory" for the character. However, not all narratives have a perfect ending — these are RESOLUTIONS. They mark the end of a journey and things are somewhat better. The conflict HAS decreased in severity, but maybe not gone away completely. Resolutions don't erase all the character's struggles or lead to a flawless outcome, but they do leave the reader with a sense of completion.

After instruction on ways to END a conflict, model how to think of POSSIBLE solutions to each problem generated from the original photographs. Again, model how to choose the BEST option — the most realistic and interesting one. Continue refining students' understanding of how to "land" a story by having them return to their own narrative quickwrites and insert a solution near the BOTTOM of the document. Task them to write only 1-or-2-sentences that reveal how the conflict was resolved, and to do this for EACH of the personal topics they've started.

NOW, the solution or resolution is PART 1 of a two-part narrative conclusion. The second element hints at a deeper theme or lesson learned. Through reflection, the character reveals personal growth or a shift in his perspective. This is a more mature element to narrative conclusions that appears in state standards, usually by 7th grade. In this reflection, the writer specifically mentions something he learned about: HIMSELF, or about relationships with OTHER people, or learned about LIFE in general.

Together, these two elements — resolve and reflect — create a satisfying and thoughtful conclusion to any narrative experience. HOWEVER, similar to holding off on teaching MULTIPLE PLOT LINES, I'd wait to introduce students to this second part of a narrative conclusion. Just target part 1 for now. Then, in a FUTURE narrative unit you can add this more nuanced element.
skill_title: Solution vs Resolution and Character Reflection

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Skill 3: Introduce Character and Setting
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Skill #3: Introduce Character and Setting

So far, we've learned that the main idea of a narrative is its plot — a problem that gets resolved. Now, pivot your instruction to how a story starts, with the revealing of character and setting (#3).

The writer must introduce the character in a specific setting BEFORE the conflict arises. This is what the standards mean by "orient the reader". It includes describing the character when life is good or all is well. Show the reader who this character is, typically. This makes the transition from NORMAL to PROBLEMATIC more impactful because it disrupts the peaceful scene the reader was just introduced to.

HOWEVER, THIS is the part of a narrative that students often OVERwrite. Let's connect back to an airplane flight: WHILE the plane doesn't go from zero to 30,000 feet immediately, nobody wants to sit on the tarmac too long either! Similarly, narratives only need a little runway — just a little background information before the conflict takes off. Consequently, caution students about overloading the exposition with excessive characterization. While this approach may produce a fantastic character sketch — it's not a STORY until there is a conflict that propels the action forward.

Now, let me clarify, there will be plenty of opportunities to develop characters in great detail within the middle of the story, and we'll talk about that momentarily in Essential Skill #4.

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Choosing Key Character and Setting Details for the Opening
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Choosing Key Character and Setting Details for the Opening

For the beginning, help students determine HOW to choose the KEY character details to include within the opening sentences. Teach them this using a 2-step process.

FIRST, model how to list ALL the possible character details, and THEN, narrow it down to 2-3 that will make THIS conflict troublesome for THAT character. Returning to the hiking photo:
— If the conflict is over sharing food and resources, then reveal the quantity of each that characters brought in their backpacks.
— If the conflict is over the difficult terrain they will face, then introduce each character's level of experience in the beginning.
— If the conflict is an individual's fear of heights, then introduce why he is heading out on a hike in the first place.

Repeat this process with the setting, choosing the most relevant details that make the pending conflict something that could only happen there and then. After practicing this with the photographs, students can return to their PERSONAL narrative topics for further experience.
skill_title: Choosing Key Character and Setting Details for the Opening

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Skill 4: Use Narrative Techniques to Sequence Details
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Skill #4: Use Narrative Techniques to Sequence Details

At this point, students understand that narratives have three basic parts: They BEGIN with the most important information or exposition about characters in a setting. They QUICKLY reveal a CONFLICT. And they SOLVE or RESOLVE it by the end.

Now, there IS a lot more to writing a sophisticated narrative, but at its CORE — those are the 3 parts or ingredients that compose the basic story arc.

When considering what skill to teach next, focus on making their narratives LONGER and STRONGER by SHAPING the characters using narrative techniques. This is ESSENTIAL SKILL #4.

There's no need to teach students how to write long narratives until they've mastered writing short ones. Once students can demonstrate their ability to write concise, focused stories that have a plot, they're ready to learn how to expand those narratives into longer, more developed pieces. And the key to creating a longer story is by stretching the middle — by prolonging the time between the conflict and its resolution. When reading literature we refer to this as the rising action.

This is a crucial concept to emphasize with students: you don't make a story longer by adding more AFTER the end; you add more to the middle. Emotions, tensions, episodes are all getting more intense — they are RISING to a breaking point. THIS is what makes a narrative engaging. And THIS is where characterization is really developed.
skill_title: Skill 4: Use Narrative Techniques to Sequence Details

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Stretching the Middle with Character Details
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Stretching the Middle with Character Details

Rather than providing a laundry list of details about the character in the beginning, the reader learns more about the character throughout the MIDDLE, throughout the struggle. These details will be much more interesting and relevant!

The secret to this longer middle is knowing what additional information to include. Teach students the various narrative techniques that further develop and shape main characters. Include the addition of his:
— thoughts and feelings
— actions and reactions, habits and decisions
— words spoken in dialogue, or communicated through texts and emails

Teach students how to weave these character details throughout the episodes of the rising action. Compare this to writing in slow motion, adding details one by one, in order and in sequence. By teaching students how to stretch the middle, they maintain the integrity of the story arc, WHILE transforming a simple narrative into a more engaging and dynamic story.
skill_title: Stretching the Middle with Character Details

section_name: Episode 8 Secondary — Pre-Writing Process and Key Takeaways
content:
Episode 8 | Narrative for Secondary — Pre-Writing Process and Key Takeaways

This process is all part of the pre-writing stage. Using a storyboard, organize the story into sections: the beginning, middle, and end. For example, in the middle section, place the problem at the far right, leaving space for the developing details. Convert this into a 5- to 9-box organizer to help students map out the key moments of the story. Remind students that the conflict sits at the beginning of the middle, setting the stage for what unfolds. Just like we planned the hiking narrative, this is the approach for any story — starting with the conflict, moving through essential character and setting information, and finishing with the resolution. Character development then unfolds in the middle. Pre-writing these details before typing the first draft is essential for a solid start. This is especially important when the narrative is being completed as an assessment in one sitting. With a clear plan in hand, students don't need to worry about what comes next — allowing their minds to focus on crafting ideas into sentences and progressing the story forward. Pre-writing these details on paper BEFORE beginning to type the first draft is key to a solid FIRST draft. And this is EVEN more important when it's done as an assessment all in one sitting. With a plan that ensures they know where their story is going, their brains take on the cognitive load of stretching ideas into sentences and not thinking about what should happen next.

When first teaching a new writing skill, it's important to give students plenty of focused practice opportunities. In this situation, it means your students will NOT crank out full narratives from beginning to end. We haven't even taught them about the beginning yet! Instead, start small. Show a photo, identify the visible character and setting, brainstorm possible problems that fit the situation, then repeat the process with different photographs. Give them lots of experience with the INDIVIDUAL skill. Then, after teaching about story solutions, return to the same original photos and problems to give them lots of practice coming up with realistic solutions.

This approach teaches students the fundamentals of narrative writing by breaking it into manageable parts. It gives them repeated experience with each INDIVIDUAL skill during the unit, before asking them to write a complete narrative at the END of the unit.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the 2 most important takeaways: FIRST, start instruction emphasizing a story's conflict and resolution — the takeoff and landing. And second, remember that characterization is more engaging when used to develop the middle — rather than all rolled out in the beginning exposition.

That said, I encourage you to apply these four essential skills when teaching your students about narrative writing, and by doing this, we take the next step toward building better writers.
